The gambler's problem

A gambler with $s$ pounds bets on coin flips until reaching £100 or going broke. Heads wins the amount staked; tails loses it. Value iteration (Lesson 33) finds the stakes that maximise the chance of reaching £100, and the answer looks nothing like a sensible betting plan.

Value estimates $V(s)$ for capital $s = 1, \ldots, 99$ after sweeps 1, 2 and 3 and after the latest sweep (S&B Figure 4.3, top). $V(s)$ is the probability of reaching £100.

Bold, timid or optimal

Play 10,000 sessions from capital $s$ (the slider above) with three strategies: bet everything you can ("bold", $a = \min(s, 100-s)$), bet £1 every time ("timid"), or follow the greedy stakes.

The maths

States are capital $s \in \{1, \ldots, 99\}$. Actions are stakes $a \in \{0, 1, \ldots, \min(s, 100 - s)\}$. The reward is $+1$ on reaching £100 and $0$ otherwise, with no discounting. So the value of a state is the probability of reaching £100 from it. Writing $V(0) = 0$ and $V(100) = 1$ for the two terminal outcomes, value iteration sweeps:

$$V(s) \leftarrow \max_{a} \Big[\, p_h\, V(s + a) + (1 - p_h)\, V(s - a) \,\Big]$$

Each capital takes the best stake's chance of winning, using the current estimates of where heads and tails lead.

For $p_h < \tfrac12$ every bet loses money on average, so fewer bets are better. In that case bold play (always stake $\min(s, 100 - s)$) is known to be optimal (Dubins and Savage), which gives some exact values:

$$\begin{aligned} v_*(50) &= p_h \\ v_*(25) &= p_h\, v_*(50) = p_h^2 \\ v_*(75) &= p_h + (1 - p_h)\, v_*(50) = p_h(2 - p_h) \end{aligned}$$

From £50 one bet wins it all. From £25 two heads in a row are needed. From £75, stake £25: heads wins, tails drops to £50.

Betting £1 every time is the classic gambler's ruin. With $r = (1 - p_h)/p_h$ and $r \ne 1$:

$$\Pr[\text{reach } 100 \mid s] = \frac{1 - r^{s}}{1 - r^{100}}$$

For $p_h = 0.4$ and $s = 50$ that is about $1.6 \times 10^{-9}$, against $0.4$ for one bold bet. For $p_h > \tfrac12$ the picture flips: each bet gains on average, small stakes let that average take hold, and the greedy stake is £1 everywhere.

The spiky policy is one of many optimal policies. Several stakes give exactly the same value, which is why S&B's Exercise 4.8 asks why the policy looks so odd.
